clinicalPearls: Presents as soft, yellowish, umbilicated papules on the forehead, cheeks and nose of middle-aged and older adults.
The central umbilication corresponds to a dilated sebaceous duct surrounded by enlarged sebaceous lobules, giving a doughnut-like configuration.
Lesions are often multiple in individuals with seborrhoeic, sun-damaged skin and in those on long-term ciclosporin after organ transplantation.
Dermoscopy shows a central crater with surrounding cream-yellow lobules and a 'crown' of unbranched or minimally branched peripheral vessels.
The crown vessels do not cross the midline of the lesion, helping to distinguish it from the arborising telangiectasia of basal cell carcinoma.
The main clinical challenge is differentiation from basal cell carcinoma, which may require dermoscopy or biopsy.
Treatment is for cosmetic reasons only and includes light electrodesiccation, laser, photodynamic therapy or topical/oral retinoids.
Widespread early-onset lesions can be a feature of the Muir-Torre syndrome, particularly when sebaceous adenomas or carcinomas coexist.
reference.pathophysiology: Sebaceous hyperplasia represents a benign enlargement of otherwise normal sebaceous glands, in which numerous mature sebaceous lobules cluster around a centrally dilated excretory duct. The process reflects reduced epidermal cell turnover and diminished androgen-driven basal sebocyte replacement with ageing, causing retention and accumulation of crowded mature sebocytes. Chronic ultraviolet exposure and immunosuppression, especially ciclosporin, accelerate the process. Although a benign hamartomatous proliferation, extensive and early lesions may reflect the sebaceous gland dysregulation seen in the Muir-Torre variant of Lynch syndrome, mediated by mismatch-repair deficiency.
additionalInvestigations: dermoscopy to demonstrate crown vessels and central umbilication
punch or shave biopsy where basal cell carcinoma cannot be excluded
histopathology confirming enlarged mature sebaceous lobules
assessment for Muir-Torre syndrome in extensive or early-onset disease
mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry on sebaceous neoplasms when syndrome suspected
redFlags: arborising telangiectasia, pearly rolled border or ulceration suggesting basal cell carcinoma
numerous sebaceous lesions at a young age suggesting Muir-Torre syndrome
a firm, rapidly growing or bleeding lesion raising concern for sebaceous carcinoma
coexisting visceral malignancy or strong family history of colorectal cancer
reference.prognosis: Sebaceous hyperplasia is entirely benign and of cosmetic significance only, although individual lesions persist and new ones accumulate with age. Recurrence after superficial destruction is common because the deeper gland is often incompletely removed.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing basal cell carcinoma as sebaceous hyperplasia and delaying appropriate treatment.
Failing to recognise the Muir-Torre association in patients with multiple or early lesions.
Aggressive destructive treatment causing scarring for a purely cosmetic lesion.
Confusing lesions with molluscum contagiosum in immunosuppressed patients.
management: Reassure, as the condition is benign and treatment is for cosmetic reasons only
Offer physical ablation of troublesome lesions by electrocautery/electrodesiccation, cryotherapy or laser
Consider topical retinoids or, for extensive disease, oral isotretinoin, recognising lesions tend to recur
In transplant recipients, discuss modifying ciclosporin-based immunosuppression with the transplant team
Advise photoprotection to limit ultraviolet-driven new lesions
Exclude basal cell carcinoma with dermoscopy or biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Evaluate for Muir-Torre syndrome in early-onset or extensive disease, with mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry
